# Showing Distributions {.divider}

[Boxplots, violins & ridgelines · Day 01]{.eyebrow}


<!-- slide 74 -->
## Choosing a Distribution Plot {.smaller}

[Showing distributions · what to plot when]{.eyebrow}

### Six lenses on a single variable

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="33%"}
![](images/plot-icons/02-distributions/01-histogram.svg){height=3.4em}

**Histogram**

Counts in bins. Raw shape; sensitive to bin width.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
![](images/plot-icons/02-distributions/02-density.svg){height=3.4em}

**Density (KDE)**

Smoothed shape. Best for overlaying a few groups.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
![](images/plot-icons/02-distributions/03-boxplot.svg){height=3.4em}

**Boxplot**

Five-number summary. Compact across many groups.
:::
::::::

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="33%"}
![](images/plot-icons/02-distributions/04-violins.svg){height=3.4em}

**Violin**

Density mirrored. Shape + summary in one footprint.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
![](images/plot-icons/02-distributions/05-strip-chart.svg){height=3.4em}

**Strip / sina**

Every point shown. Honest when n is small.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
![](images/plot-icons/02-distributions/07-ridgeline.svg){height=3.4em}

**Ridgeline**

Distributions stacked across groups or time.
:::
::::::

::: {.takeaway}
[Rule of thumb]{.tl}
**Small n → strip · few groups → density or histogram · many groups → boxplot or ridgeline · need shape *and* summary → violin.**
:::


<!-- slide 75 -->
## When & Why a Boxplot {.smaller}

[Distributions · when to use]{.eyebrow}

### A boxplot summarises spread, pick the chart that fits your question

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
Use a boxplot to compare the **distribution** of a continuous value across a few
groups — its centre, spread, and outliers — without plotting every point.

**Spread is not precision.** SD describes how the data scatter around the mean;
SE describes how precise your estimate of the mean is. A boxplot answers the
first question; error bars on a mean answer the second.

```python
r = np.random.default_rng(1)
groups = ["WT", "Mut A", "Mut B"]
data = [r.normal(50, 6, 70),                # WT
        r.normal(62, 10, 70),               # Mut A — bigger spread
        r.normal(58, 4, 70)]                # Mut B — tighter
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 5
r = np.random.default_rng(1)
groups = ["WT", "Mut A", "Mut B"]
data = [r.normal(50, 6, 70), r.normal(62, 10, 70), r.normal(58, 4, 70)]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5))
bp = ax.boxplot(data, widths=0.55, patch_artist=True, labels=groups)
for p in bp["boxes"]: p.set_facecolor(ECON["hongkong"][3]); p.set_edgecolor(GREEN)
for m in bp["medians"]: m.set_color(INK); m.set_linewidth(2)
for w in bp["whiskers"] + bp["caps"]: w.set_color(GREEN)
for fl in bp["fliers"]: fl.set(marker="o", markerfacecolor=CREAM, markeredgecolor=RED, markersize=5)
ax.set_ylabel("Expression (TPM)")
ax.set_title("DISTRIBUTION ACROSS THREE GENOTYPES", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=INK, pad=10)
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}
SD vs SE: spread of the **data** vs precision of the **estimate**. Same numbers,
different question, different chart. *(Wilke 2019, Ch. 9)*
:::

## Building a Boxplot · Step 2: the raw points {.smaller}

[Distributions · boxplot build]{.eyebrow}

### Look at the data first, with a little horizontal jitter

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
Plot every observation, jittering x-position so points don't stack on one line.
This shows the sample size and shape that a summary will later hide.

```python {code-line-numbers="2-7"}
# data: list of three np.ndarrays, one per group
rj = np.random.default_rng(2)
for i, d in enumerate(data, start=1):
    x = rj.normal(i, 0.06, len(d))           # gentle jitter
    ax.scatter(x, d,
               color=GREEN, s=18,
               alpha=0.5, edgecolors="none")
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}

#| out-width: "100%"

ax.set_ylabel("Expression (TPM)"); ax.set_xticks([1, 2, 3]); ax.set_xticklabels(groups)
ax.set_xlim(0.5, 3.5); ax.set_ylim(30, 85)

for i, d in enumerate(data, start=1):
    ax.scatter(rj.normal(i, 0.06, len(d)), d, color=GREEN, s=18, alpha=0.5, edgecolors="none")
```

## Building a Boxplot · Step 3: add the box {.smaller}

[Distributions · boxplot build]{.eyebrow}

### Overlay the five-number summary on top of the points

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
The box draws Q1 → Q3, the median line, and whiskers to the most extreme points
within 1.5 × IQR. Matplotlib computes all of it for you.

```python {code-line-numbers="1-6"}
bp = ax.boxplot(
    data,
    positions=[1, 2, 3],
    widths=0.5,
    patch_artist=True,        # so we can colour it
)
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}

    ax.scatter(rj.normal(i, 0.06, len(d)), d, color=GREEN, s=18, alpha=0.35, edgecolors="none")

ax.set_title("STEP 3: ADD THE BOX (DEFAULT)", fontsize=12, fontweight="bold", color=INK, pad=10)
```

## Building a Boxplot · Step 5: the message {.smaller}

[Distributions · boxplot build]{.eyebrow}

### Hide duplicate outliers, title the finding

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
The points already show every value, so turn off the default flier markers.
Finish with a title that says what the reader should take away.

```python {code-line-numbers="1-2"}
bp = ax.boxplot(data, showfliers=False, ...)
ax.set_title("MUT A SHOWS THE WIDEST SPREAD")
```

That's the whole recipe: **canvas → points → box → style → message.**
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
```

<!-- slide 81 -->
## When & Why a Violin {.smaller}

[Distributions · when to use]{.eyebrow}

### Reach for a violin when the shape matters, not just the summary

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
A boxplot hides shape — two very different distributions can share the same
five-number summary. A violin draws a **mirrored density**, so a second hump or
a long skew is visible at a glance.

Use it when the distribution might be **bimodal** or strongly skewed. Use a
plain boxplot when a clean five-number summary is all you need.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 5
r = np.random.default_rng(3)
bimodal = np.concatenate([r.normal(45, 5, 45), r.normal(62, 5, 35)])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5))
vp = ax.violinplot([bimodal], positions=[1], widths=0.7, showextrema=False)
for b in vp["bodies"]:
    b.set_facecolor(ECON["hongkong"][3]); b.set_edgecolor(GREEN); b.set_alpha(0.85)
bx = ax.boxplot([bimodal], positions=[1], widths=0.12, patch_artist=True, showfliers=False)
for p in bx["boxes"]: p.set_facecolor(INK)
for m in bx["medians"]: m.set_color(CREAM)
ax.set_xticks([1]); ax.set_xticklabels(["one sample"]); ax.set_ylabel("Expression (TPM)")
ax.set_title("THE BOX MISSES THE TWO PEAKS", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=INK, pad=10)
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}
The boxplot shows the summary. The violin shows the **shape**. Bimodality is the
story the box can't tell. *(Wilke 2019, Ch. 7)*
:::

## Building a Violin · Step 5: the message {.smaller}

[Distributions · violin build]{.eyebrow}

### Slim inner boxplot for the summary, title the finding

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
A thin boxplot inside each violin gives the five-number summary and the shape
together. Finish with the takeaway in the title.

```python {code-line-numbers="1-7"}
for i, d in enumerate(data, start=1):
    bx = ax.boxplot(d, positions=[i],
                    widths=0.1, patch_artist=True,
                    showfliers=False)

ax.set_title("WT IS BIMODAL")
```

Same recipe as the box: **canvas → points → density → style → message.**

```{python}
#| fig-height: 4.7

ax.set_ylim(25, 85); ax.set_ylabel("Expression (TPM)")
```

<!-- slide 87 -->
## Ridgeline · The Data {.smaller}

[Distributions · ridgeline]{.eyebrow}

### 2,000 single cells, ordered along a trajectory

`load_pseudotime()` is single-cell data in tidy long form: **one row per cell**. Each cell has a pseudotime `stage` (1 = earliest, 8 = latest along the differentiation path) and the marker gene's `expression`. With 250 cells per stage, every stage is a proper distribution, not a single number.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
from genomics_course.data import load_pseudotime

pt = load_pseudotime()        # cell, stage, expression
print(pt.shape)               # 2000 cells × 3 columns
pt.head(4)
```


<!-- slide 88 -->
## Ridgeline · See the Cells First {.smaller}

[Distributions · ridgeline]{.eyebrow}

### Before any smoothing: one dot per cell

Plot every cell as a dot, expression on the x-axis, stage on the y-axis with a little jitter. Early stages sit in a low cloud (gene OFF); late stages sit in a high cloud (gene ON); the middle stages show **both clouds at once**, that's the bimodal hand-off. The ridgeline next just replaces each row of dots with a smooth density.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "8-12"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 5.0
from genomics_course.data import load_pseudotime

pt = load_pseudotime()                                     # 2000 cells: cell, stage, expression
stages = sorted(pt.stage.unique())                         # ordered pseudotime stages 1..8
n = len(stages)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)                             # reproducible jitter

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5.0))
for i, s in enumerate(stages):                             # one row of dots per stage
    vals = pt.loc[pt.stage == s, "expression"].values      # this stage's cells
    y = i + rng.uniform(-0.32, 0.32, len(vals))            # jitter so dots don't pile on one line
    ax.scatter(vals, y, s=6, color=econ_spectrum(i / (n - 1)),  # x = expression, one dot per cell
               alpha=.35, linewidths=0)                    # low alpha shows where cells pile up
ax.set_yticks(range(n)); ax.set_yticklabels([f"stage {s}" for s in stages], fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("NEUROD1 expression"); ax.set_ylabel("pseudotime →")
ax.set_xlim(0, 12)
for sp in ["top", "right", "left"]:                        # bare frame, same look as the ridgeline
    ax.spines[sp].set_visible(False)
ax.set_title("each dot is one cell", color=MUTED, fontsize=11, loc="left")
plt.show()
```

<!-- slide 89 -->
# Ridgelines {.divider}

[Many distributions, one panel · Day 01]{.eyebrow}


<!-- slide 90 -->
## When a Ridgeline {.smaller}

[Distributions · theory]{.eyebrow}

### Watch a distribution change across an ordered factor

A ridgeline stacks one density per group, slightly overlapping, so you compare many distributions in a compact panel. It earns its place when the groups have a **meaningful order** and the distribution *shifts* across it: expression along pseudotime, a signal across tissues, a metric over time. The **shape** is the story, a mode appearing, a peak sliding right.

Two requirements keep it honest: enough points per group for a smooth density (a KDE on twenty values is noise), and a colour ramp **keyed to the group order** so the eye follows the progression instead of decoding a rainbow. Here: a neural marker switching on as cells differentiate.


<!-- slide 91 -->
## Ridgeline · The Data {.smaller}

[Distributions · ridgeline]{.eyebrow}

### A marker gene across single cells, ordered by pseudotime

`load_pseudotime()` is tidy long: one row per cell, its pseudotime `stage` (1 = earliest), and the marker's `expression`. Each stage is a distribution we'll turn into one ridge.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
from genomics_course.data import load_pseudotime

pt = load_pseudotime()   # cell, stage, expression
pt.head(4)
```


<!-- slide 92 -->
## Ridgeline · Step 1 — A Density Per Stage {.smaller}

[Distributions · build]{.eyebrow}

### 1 · KDE each group

Smooth each stage's expression into a density with `gaussian_kde`, on a shared x-grid, and normalise to the same height so shapes are comparable. Overlaid, you can already see a second hump appear, but they collide.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "9-12"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 4.7
from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde                       # kernel density estimator
from genomics_course.data import load_pseudotime

pt = load_pseudotime()                                     # cell, stage, expression
stages = sorted(pt.stage.unique())                         # ordered pseudotime stages 1..8
xs = np.linspace(0, 12, 300)                               # shared grid for every density

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.7))                 # one panel
for s in stages:                                           # one KDE per stage
    vals = pt.loc[pt.stage == s, "expression"].values      # this stage's cells
    k = gaussian_kde(vals)(xs)                              # smooth density over xs
    ax.plot(xs, k / k.max(), color=GREEN, lw=1.2, alpha=.6)  # normalise height; all overlaid
ax.set_xlabel("NEUROD1 expression"); ax.set_ylabel("density (normalised)")
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide 93 -->
## Ridgeline · Step 2 — Stack the Ridges {.smaller}

[Distributions · build]{.eyebrow}

### 2 · Offset and fill

Give each density its own baseline `y = i` and `fill_between` it, scaled by `overlap` (>1 so neighbours touch). Colour by stage along `econ_spectrum`, and the `zorder` puts lower ridges in front. Now they read as a stack.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "7,12-15"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 5.2
from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde
from genomics_course.data import load_pseudotime

pt = load_pseudotime()                                     # cell, stage, expression
stages = sorted(pt.stage.unique())                         # ordered stages
xs = np.linspace(0, 12, 300)                               # shared grid
n = len(stages); overlap = 1.8                             # ridge height (>1 → ridges overlap)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5.2))
for i, s in enumerate(stages):                             # stage 1 at the bottom, 8 at the top
    vals = pt.loc[pt.stage == s, "expression"].values      # this stage's cells
    k = gaussian_kde(vals)(xs); k = k / k.max() * overlap  # normalise, then scale to ridge height
    col = econ_spectrum(i / (n - 1))                       # colour keyed to pseudotime order
    ax.fill_between(xs, i + k, i, color=col, alpha=.8,     # ridge sits on baseline y = i
                    lw=1, edgecolor=CREAM, zorder=n - i)    # lower ridges drawn in front
ax.set_yticks(range(n)); ax.set_yticklabels([f"stage {s}" for s in stages], fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("NEUROD1 expression"); ax.set_ylabel("pseudotime →")
ax.set_xlim(0, 12)
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide 94 -->
## Ridgeline · Step 3 — The Message {.smaller}

[Distributions · build]{.eyebrow}

### 3 · Clean edge, no frame, name the finding

Trace each ridge's top in cream so overlaps stay crisp, drop the frame (ridgelines read better bare), and title with the result. The OFF→bimodal→ON march is the whole point.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "15,19-22"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 5.2
from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde
from genomics_course.data import load_pseudotime

pt = load_pseudotime()                                     # cell, stage, expression
stages = sorted(pt.stage.unique())                         # ordered stages
xs = np.linspace(0, 12, 300)                               # shared grid
n = len(stages); overlap = 1.8                             # ridge height

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5.2))
for i, s in enumerate(stages):                             # bottom → top
    vals = pt.loc[pt.stage == s, "expression"].values      # this stage's cells
    k = gaussian_kde(vals)(xs); k = k / k.max() * overlap  # normalised, scaled density
    col = econ_spectrum(i / (n - 1))                       # spectrum keyed to order
    ax.fill_between(xs, i + k, i, color=col, alpha=.8, lw=1, edgecolor=CREAM, zorder=n - i)
    ax.plot(xs, i + k, color=CREAM, lw=.8, zorder=n - i)   # crisp cream top edge per ridge
ax.set_yticks(range(n)); ax.set_yticklabels([f"stage {s}" for s in stages], fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("NEUROD1 expression"); ax.set_ylabel("pseudotime →")
ax.set_xlim(0, 12); ax.set_ylim(-0.3, n + overlap)         # headroom for the top ridge
for sp in ["top", "right", "left"]:                        # ridgelines read better frameless
    ax.spines[sp].set_visible(False)
ax.set_title("NEUROD1 SWITCHES ON ALONG THE TRAJECTORY",   # title states the finding
             color=GREEN, fontweight="bold", loc="left")
plt.show()
```

::: {.takeaway}
[The bottom line]{.tl}
A ridgeline is many densities stacked along an ordered factor: **KDE each group → offset and fill → ramp keyed to order**. Watch the marker switch on, a single OFF hump, a bimodal transition where some cells flip, then a single ON hump. The shift *is* the result.
:::
